Jersey City offices that handle property tax

Jersey City splits the work between a Tax Assessor, who sets and records values, and a Tax Collector, who sends the bills and takes payment. The collector's counter is at 280 Grove Street, Room 101, and serves the public each business day between 8:30 and 4:30. Mail goes to the City of Jersey City Tax Collector at that address, with checks or money orders made out to the same name. The city's property tax page also lists online payment and a bank-debit option that uses a signed authorization form.

To look up an assessment, open the state-hosted tax records site, choose Hudson County and Jersey City, then search by street address, owner name or block and lot. The assessor's page also links the forms most sellers and heirs end up needing, including veteran deduction claims, exemption claims and the five-year exemption and abatement application.

Due dates and installments

Jersey City bills fall on the first of February, May, August and November, matching the state schedule in N.J.S.A. 54:4-66. Ask the collector how much grace the city allows before you count on paying a few days late.

Jersey City installments and how each amount is set
InstallmentDue dateHow the amount is figured
FirstFebruary 1One quarter of the prior year's tax
SecondMay 1One quarter of the prior year's tax
ThirdAugust 1Half of the current levy left after the first two payments
FourthNovember 1The other half of that remaining current levy

A missed quarter stays delinquent, with interest, until every tax and lien due on the property is cleared. Paying ahead is allowed, and interest only starts after the delinquency date.

Jersey City's tax rate

The Division of Taxation's 2025 table gives Jersey City a general rate of 2.335 and an effective rate of 1.847. The effective rate restates that levy against estimated full value, which makes it the fairer yardstick when you compare towns.

The city's last full revaluation of every property took place in 2017, carried out in response to a state order. Assessments since then are updated by the assessor's office. Before listing, pull the latest assessment for your block and lot and set it beside recent nearby sale prices.

Can I appeal a Jersey City assessment?

Yes, through the Hudson County Board of Taxation rather than any city office. The assessor's page links the county petition and its instructions, and the county accepts filings online, in person on Cornelison Avenue, or by mail after a call to (201) 395-6260. Revaluation shifted every Jersey City assessment in 2017, which makes the facts behind an old appeal worth rechecking today. The main points:

  • Cutoff: April 1, or May 1 after a revaluation or reassessment, with extra time when notices are mailed late.
  • Proof: sales from before the October 1 assessment date, with photographs, carry the argument.
  • Attendance: skipping the hearing can produce a dismissal that also closes the door to Tax Court.
  • Payoff: a reduction holds for the appeal year and the two after it.

Jersey City housing snapshot

Jersey City had 292,449 residents in the 2020 census on 14.74 square miles of land, and the 2025 estimate stands at 302,013. Owners live in just 27.9 percent of the homes. For 2020 to 2024 the middle owned home was worth $566,900, rent in the middle ran $2,007 and a typical household brought in $97,710.

Most neighbors rent, so a house with tenants is a common situation. A buyer will want the lease, the rent roll and any open repair requests, and unpaid tax on a rental parcel creates the same lien risk as on an owner-occupied one.

Location, water and flood exposure

Jersey City is the Hudson County seat, framed by the Hudson River and Upper New York Bay to the east and the Hackensack River and Newark Bay to the west. Buyers search by neighborhood name: Paulus Hook and the downtown waterfront, Journal Square, Bergen Hill, the Heights and Greenville in the south. The city connects to Manhattan through the Holland Tunnel, PATH, NJ Transit buses and NY Waterway ferries, so expect questions about distance to PATH, buses and ferries when you list.

The waterfront has a flood record, since Hurricane Irene's storm surge flooded parts of downtown in August 2011. Check flood exposure on a waterfront or low block before you price the house or discuss repairs.

Handling tax owed on a Jersey City house

Start with the assessment search so you know the block and lot on record, then ask the collector for the balance by quarter. Three items cause most surprises: a quarter that went delinquent, a tax lien held by a third party, and a bill for an abatement payment, which the city's payment page routes to its own portal. If the house has a five-year exemption or abatement, confirm that its payment is current before closing.

  • Bring the block and lot, the owner's name and the property address when you call the collector.
  • Ask for a written payoff figure good through the closing date.
  • Ask the assessor whether a veteran or senior deduction on the property ends with the sale.
  • Inherited houses may carry unpaid quarters from before the owner's death, so check them first.

The closing agent pays the confirmed balance from your proceeds. A cash buyer skips the mortgage process, but the tax and lien check does not go away.

A workable timeline looks like this. When you decide to sell, pull the assessment and the block and lot. Before you sign a contract, get the collector's balance by quarter and ask about any lien. As the closing date nears, request an updated written payoff that runs through that date, because interest changes the number. At the table, the title company pays the confirmed amount and records the payment. If any item looks wrong, ask the collector or the assessor to explain it before you sign, not after. Keep copies of every written payoff, deduction notice and receipt, and give the closing agent the same set you hold, so everyone is working from one version of the numbers.

Sellers who inherited a house should also bring the paperwork that shows who now owns it, since the assessor's record and the collector's bill both follow the owner of record. If the old owner's name is still on the account, the payoff request can be slowed until the records match.

Tenants add one more step, and it is easy to forget when the closing date is close. If a renter lives in the house, give the buyer the lease and tell the collector where bills should be mailed so no notice goes to the wrong address.

Frequently asked questions

What are the due dates for property tax in Jersey City?

Four dates a year: the first of February, May, August and November. The collector can confirm any grace period.

Where can I pay a Jersey City property tax bill in person?

The Tax Collector's office is at 280 Grove Street, Room 101, and serves walk-in payers each business day between 8:30 and 4:30. Online and mailed payments are accepted too.

How do I look up my Jersey City assessment?

Open the tax records site linked on the assessor's page, select Hudson County and Jersey City, then search by address, owner or block and lot.

When did Jersey City last revalue every property?

In 2017, following a state order. The assessor's office has maintained values since.

Does a Jersey City appeal go to the city or the county?

The county board hears it, and the city does not. Its usual cutoff is April 1, with May 1 applying after a revaluation.

Who sends the Newark property tax bill?

Newark's Department of Finance does both jobs, sending the bill and collecting the money. Essex County gets involved only if an owner contests the assessed value. Two units inside Finance matter to a seller. Assessments decides which real estate is taxable, keeps a map of each parcel and logs changes in ownership and mortgages. Revenue Collections mails the bills, takes payments and chases accounts that fall behind.

Customer service answers questions about a balance Monday through Friday, 9 am to 4 pm, except holidays. The tax lines are 973-733-3791, 973-733-3792, 973-733-3962, 973-733-8098 and 973-733-3978. The Payment Center on the city website takes tax payments by credit card, debit card or electronic check. Sellers should phone before the first showing, so the balance is known long before a contract arrives. Most seller questions come down to timing: when the next installment falls due, what is still open, and whether anything has already gone to a tax sale.

Due dates and penalties

Four installments make up the year, and the dates match the quarterly schedule used all over New Jersey. Interest builds on late amounts, and a big delinquency can draw an extra penalty at year end.

Newark quarterly due dates with the interest ceiling for late payments
InstallmentDue dateHighest interest on a late amount
FirstFebruary 18 percent on the first $1,500 owed, 18 percent on the rest
SecondMay 1Same limits
ThirdAugust 1Same limits
FourthNovember 1Same limits

When the fiscal year closes, a delinquency above $10,000 may add a penalty, capped at 6 percent.

Newark credits a partial payment to the oldest quarter still open. Suppose an owner is behind three quarters and mails a check in September: it reduces the first quarter's principal and interest, and the later quarters stay unpaid. As a result, the payoff figure on a closing statement may be bigger than a quick add-up of the latest bill would suggest.

What happens to a Newark house when taxes go unpaid?

A tax lien certificate on the house goes up for sale. Newark holds a standard sale for earlier years' taxes and charges still owed, plus an accelerated sale for current-year charges left unpaid after the statutory date of November 10. N.J.S.A. 54:5-19 is the state law behind prior-year balances.

  • Whoever buys the certificate gets a lien, not title to the house.
  • Six months after the sale a town holder may sue to foreclose, while a private holder must wait two years.
  • Before final judgment the owner may demand in writing a sheriff's sale, which protects any equity above the debt.
  • The right to redeem lasts until the Superior Court enters a judgment cutting it off.

Our separate New Jersey tax sale guide goes deeper on redemption costs and how to make the equity demand.

How to appeal your Newark assessment

File Form A-1 with the Essex County Board of Taxation, along with its companion comparable sales form. The board must have the petition in hand by April 1, or by May 1 if Newark has just completed a revaluation or reassessment. If the assessed value tops $1,000,000, the owner can bypass the board and file with the State Tax Court.

Proof falls on the owner, who must show that the assessed value is unreasonable next to market value. To count as excessive or discriminatory, an assessment has to miss on two tests at once: the true market value standard and the common level range, a band of 15 percent around the district's average ratio.

  • You get 45 days after a county board judgment to take the case to the Tax Court of New Jersey.
  • Added or omitted assessments, which follow changes made to a property after October 1, are contested on Form AA-1.
  • An added assessment totaling more than $750,000 may be taken directly to the Tax Court.

An owner still deciding whether to appeal should weigh the calendar. A petition filed before the deadline can run alongside a sale, but the closing attorney needs to know it exists, because a ruling may alter the bill the new owner pays.

Newark housing at a glance

Newark is the largest city in New Jersey and the seat of Essex County. The estimate for July 2025 is 323,808 residents on 24.14 square miles of land. Owners occupy just 24.4 percent of homes. An owned home has a middle value of $373,700, the median gross rent is $1,392, and the 113,384 households have a median income of $52,060.

With so many renters, a seller frequently has tenants in place, and any buyer will ask to read the leases. Newark has five wards. Heavy industrial land around the airport and seaport lies mostly in the East and South wards, while residential blocks cluster in the North, Central and West.

A listing gains from nearby transit. Newark Penn Station serves PATH, NJ Transit and Amtrak, and the Newark Light Rail connects it with Broad Street Station. About 40.3 percent of Newark households had no car in 2020, so buyers often value a short walk to a train.

Rental buildings make up a large share of what trades in the city, so buyers often arrive with investor questions about leases, rent rolls and occupancy. A seller who answers those up front, with documents in hand, usually keeps a deal moving. An owner selling a house to a household will face mainly the tax payoff and the usual closing steps.

Selling with taxes owed

Before listing, request a written statement from Revenue Collections that lists each unpaid quarter, accrued interest and any tax sale certificate, calculated to the day of closing. The closing agent pays that balance from the seller's proceeds, and the lien is cleared for the buyer. If the total looks larger than you expected, ask Revenue Collections to break it out by quarter so you can see where the partial-payment rule applied. That breakdown also helps your attorney explain the figure to the buyer's side.

  • Write down every open quarter, prior-year balances included, because older amounts may already be in a tax sale.
  • Find out whether a certificate has been sold and recorded, and by whom it is held.
  • Mention a pending assessment appeal to your closing attorney so it is handled with the rest of the closing.
  • Set money aside for the transfer fee, which falls on the seller at recording.

What should you line up before closing?

Begin with the payoff. After Finance issues the written statement, give it to your attorney or title company so the exact figure, interest included, can be wired on closing day. If a certificate was sold, its holder releases the lien once paid, and the buyer gets clean title.

Then collect your papers: the most recent tax bill, any county board notice if you filed an appeal, and the name of each mortgage holder. With tenants in the house, add the leases to the pile.

Selling for cash as-is spares you repairs, showings and a lender's appraisal, yet every tax step above still happens. The balance is still paid from proceeds, and the lien must still be cleared before the deed is handed over. Pinning down the number early is what protects your closing date. Finance answers the phones on weekdays only, so plan the request around those hours.

Frequently asked questions

Where can I learn the amount owed on a Newark house?

Newark Finance customer service takes calls on weekdays from 9 am to 4 pm. Try 973-733-3791, one of five tax lines, and ask for the figure through your closing date.

By what date must a Newark assessment petition arrive?

Form A-1 goes to the Essex County Board of Taxation, and it must arrive by April 1 (May 1 after a revaluation or reassessment). Anyone assessed above $1,000,000 can bypass the board and file with the Tax Court.

What interest does Newark charge on late taxes?

Under state law, late interest tops out at 8 percent on the first $1,500 and 18 percent on whatever is left. Add a penalty of up to 6 percent if the delinquency is over $10,000 at year end.

Does paying part of my bill stop a tax sale?

Only partly. Newark applies it to the oldest quarter first, so that quarter's principal and interest shrink while later quarters stay open. A certificate can still be sold for prior-year taxes that remain unpaid.

Can I sell a Newark house that has a tax sale certificate on it?

Yes. The certificate amount and interest are paid from your sale price at closing, and the holder then discharges the lien. Ask the tax collector for a written payoff, because the title company must wire the exact figure.

Which Edison offices send and collect the tax bill

Over 30,000 tax accounts, and about as many sewer accounts, run through Edison's Tax Collector. Walk-in service is on the second floor of the municipal building, 100 Municipal Blvd., on weekdays from 8 a.m. until 4:30 in the afternoon, and the office answers 732-248-7228 and TaxCollector@EdisonNJ.gov. The Tax Assessor, a separate office, keeps data on more than 28,000 properties and takes the state deduction applications.

Because Edison lies in Middlesex County, a formal challenge to value is heard by that county's tax board. The collector cannot change a value, and the assessor cannot take a payment, so the first call depends on whether your question is about the amount of value or the amount due.

  • Collector: bills, receipts, payoff figures and sewer accounts.
  • Assessor: ownership records, property data, mailing address changes and deductions.
  • County board: formal appeals of value.

Edison at a glance

Edison is a township of roughly 109,000 people in the Raritan Valley, wrapped around the borough of Metuchen and about 27 miles from both Midtown Manhattan and Trenton. The 2025 estimate is 109,077 people. The typical home value is $496,900, owners live in 60.6 percent of homes, and median gross rent is $1,974.

Neighborhood names on a listing include Menlo Park, Oak Tree, Clara Barton, Stelton, Raritan Manor and Lincoln Park. Route 1, Route 27, Route 440 and Interstate 287 cross Edison, and the New Jersey Turnpike has its Exit 10 here. Two high schools, Edison High in the south and J.P. Stevens in the north, split the public school district of 19 schools. Winters bring snow every year and summers run hot and humid, so roof, gutter and drainage condition tend to come up in inspections.

Due dates and late interest

Edison's four installments land on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, each followed by ten days of grace that stretch to Monday when the tenth falls on a weekend. Bills go out once a year, usually in June or July, with four stubs: August and November of the current year and February and May of the next. If no bill has arrived by August 1, call the collector, because a missing bill still leaves you responsible.

A late payment accrues interest of up to 8 percent annually on $1,500 and 18 percent on the remainder, measured from the original due date after grace ends. Total delinquency past $10,000 at year end can add a surcharge of up to 6 percent. Any municipal charge still unpaid on November 11 is subject to the tax sale.

How to pay, and what a mortgage escrow changes

Options include cash, check or money order at the counter upstairs, the curbside drop box, a mailed check, or the online payment page linked from the township site. A mailed check counts when it lands in the office, whatever the postmark says, and drop box deposits post the following business day. Write checks to Edison Tax Collector, leave off any future date, and plan for a $20 fee if one bounces.

  • With an escrow account, the lender gets the original bill and you get an advice copy.
  • Paid off your mortgage? You can use the advice copy to make the next payment and tell the collector who now pays.
  • Want a mailed receipt? Return the whole bill with a prepaid return envelope.

The Edison sewer bill

One sewer bill goes out each year, drawn from the previous year's water consumption, and it can be paid in two halves. Stub one carries its own due date, usually in the April to June stretch, and stub two falls due October 1. The owner is responsible, and sewer sits outside the monthly mortgage payment.

Residential customers get a 15 percent outside water discount that is already taken off the bill. A rate freeze on a primary residence goes to owners 65 and up who show proof of age by March 1, and signing up for a Senior Center card counts as proof. At a sale, the sewer bill passes to the buyer or title company, which makes it worth confirming that both accounts are current.

Can you contest an Edison assessment?

A petition goes to the Middlesex County Board of Taxation. It is due April 1, shifting to May 1 after a township revaluation, and it must arrive by then. Copies go to the Edison assessor and clerk. The case turns on value alone, argued with as many as five comparable sales priced as of the previous October 1.

Fees scale with assessed value from $5 to $150, and a board judgment stays in force for three tax years unless something alters the assessment. Call the Middlesex board for its hearing schedule, and the Edison assessor for questions on the property record card. The assessor's office also processes the $250 deductions for a qualified veteran, seniors and disabled owners, plus the full exemption for a 100 percent disabled veteran.

What if Edison tax is owed when the house sells?

A house can sell with tax unpaid. The closing agent settles the amount out of the sale money, working from a payoff the collector dates for closing day. Ask for the per-day interest too, because a short delay moves the number.

A balance left after the November installment can become a lien, the lien has to be redeemed before a sale, and a lien holder may start foreclosure once two years pass. In Edison, a balance left on November 11 is eligible for the tax sale. Settling it before listing keeps the sale simpler, and the Tax Collector can also tell you whether the sewer account carries a balance of its own. Sewer charges unpaid on November 11 face the same tax sale exposure as property tax. For a quick look at an account, the township's tax record search shows the current status.

Steps to take before you list an Edison house

Call the Tax Collector for a payoff dated to the day you expect to close, and ask for the per-day interest as well. Check whether the sewer account has a balance of its own. Then ask the Tax Assessor for the property record card and compare it with the house. Wrong square footage or a missing note about condition can be fixed informally before it becomes an appeal.

If you have a mortgage escrow, tell the lender about the sale so the advice copy and the original bill do not cross. When the loan is paid off at closing, the next installment becomes the buyer's responsibility, and the title company needs your latest bill to place it correctly. Keep your receipts for the year in one folder, since they settle any question about what was paid before closing.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Edison Tax Collector's address?

On the second floor of the municipal building at 100 Municipal Blvd., Edison, NJ 08817, open weekdays until 4:30 p.m. The phone is 732-248-7228.

How long is the Edison tax grace period?

Ten days, counted from the due date on the stub, with a weekend ending pushed to Monday.

When is the second Edison sewer payment due?

October 1. Stub one shows the due date for the first half, usually in spring.

Does a postmark count for an Edison payment?

No. The office must receive the payment by the end of the grace period, and drop box payments are posted the next business day.

Which county board hears Edison appeals?

The Middlesex County Board of Taxation, by April 1, or May 1 after a township-wide revaluation.

Call ext. 1220 or read the date on your stub to learn when each quarter's grace period ends before you mail anything. The office does not honor postmarks. A payment has to reach the office, the drop box or the online portal by the last day of grace, and anything later carries interest running from the original due date.

The drop box sits just inside the Newark Street entrance of City Hall. The office itself shuts on city holidays and weekends.

Hoboken's tax rate

The state's 2025 table lists Hoboken at a general rate of 1.805 and an effective rate of 1.070, the lowest effective rate among the twelve Hudson County municipalities in that table. The general rate is charged on every hundred dollars of assessed value. The effective rate restates the burden against estimated true value, which lets owners compare towns whose assessments sit at different levels.

The city introduced a $152 million municipal budget for 2026 and projected a municipal tax impact of under 19 percent, or roughly $130 more per quarter for the average assessed property compared with 2025. The final figure shows on your own bill, so lean on that when you plan a sale.

How to contest a Hoboken assessment

Appeals go to the Hudson County Board of Taxation, and the Hoboken assessor's page carries the appeal forms. The state sets April 1 as the usual cutoff, or May 1 if the city completes a revaluation. A petition should include three to five comparable sales that predate the October 1 assessment date, plus photos.

The collector's page spells out how a county judgment reaches your account:

  • Nothing can be calculated until the county certifies the tax rate.
  • The credit lands on fourth-quarter tax first, then on any unpaid third-quarter balance.
  • If credit remains, it is refunded to the petitioner or to the lawyer who filed for them.
  • The next year's first two quarters reflect the lower figure, and a revised bill goes to the owner and the mortgage company on record.

Charges outside the quarterly cycle

A few charges do not follow the four-stub pattern, and each one can surface during a sale.

  • Added assessment and omitted tax bills. These cover improvements that raised a property's value. They are mailed in October and due November 1, with a grace period through November 10 and interest from November 1 after that.
  • Lien redemptions. Ask the collector for a redemption statement before you pay. Balances shown on the city website can lag, and payment must be by certified check or money order.
  • Returned checks. City ordinance DR-400 adds a $20 fee for a bounced check, and the office then asks for certified funds, cash or a money order.
  • Change of address. A signed request goes to the assessor at 94 Washington Street, by email, or by phone at ext. 1230.

Relief for Hoboken homeowners

The county hosts one combined relief application, and the Hoboken assessor handles the local deduction forms.

The state's $250 senior and disabled deduction asks for a year of New Jersey residence, ownership and occupancy of the home on October 1, and income under the limit. Once granted it must be renewed with Form PD5, filed with the collector by March 1. If you are selling, ask the assessor what happens to a deduction when the deed transfers.

Hoboken housing snapshot

The 2020 count put 60,419 people onto Hoboken's 1.25 square miles, and the newest federal estimate is 59,027. About one home in three, 33.8 percent, is lived in by its owner. For 2020 to 2024 those owned homes had a median value of $895,100, and renters paid a median $2,938 in gross rent.

Small households, a renter majority and high values shape the market, so a buyer is often an investor or a commuter weighing the monthly tax against rent. Most sales happen on the street grid of named avenues crossing numbered streets.

Selling a Hoboken house with taxes owed

A quarter left unpaid after its grace period becomes delinquent and keeps accruing interest until all taxes and liens are paid. A seller with a past-due balance has to clear it or have the closing pay it. Request a written payoff or redemption figure from the collector close to the closing date, since interest changes the number. If you renovated, ask whether any added assessment bill is still on the way.

Taxes paid ahead of a due date are accepted at any time under the statute, and no interest builds before the delinquency date. A condominium owner should also confirm whether the Special Improvement District charge sits on the bill.

Here is a simple order of work for the weeks before closing:

  • Call the collector at ext. 1220 and ask for the current balance by quarter.
  • Ask for a redemption statement if any lien exists on the parcel.
  • Hand the written figure to the title company so it can be paid from your proceeds.
  • Ask the assessor whether a deduction or added assessment will change the next bill.

Even a quick cash sale ends with a deed recorded at the county, so settle the tax status before that step.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I call to pay or ask about a Hoboken tax bill?

Phone the Tax Collector at (201) 420-2000, ext. 1220. Staff at 94 Washington Street answer on weekdays, and the office is shut on city holidays.

Are Hoboken property taxes paid quarterly?

Yes. Four stubs come with the annual bill, and each is tied to a quarterly due date. Because the office takes no postmarks, send early enough for the money to land inside the grace period.

Is Hoboken's tax rate high?

On the state's measure it is the lowest in Hudson County: 1.070 effective, lowest of the twelve towns. High home values still produce sizable bills.

What happens if my Hoboken appeal succeeds after I already paid?

Expect a credit rather than an instant check. It goes against the later quarters first and any excess is refunded, but only after the county certifies the rate.

Can I sell a Hoboken house with tax still owed?

Yes, provided the closing pays what is owing. Ask the collector for a current payoff and, if a lien exists, a redemption statement, since posted website balances can lag.

Which Cherry Hill office sends the tax bill

Property tax in Cherry Hill is billed and collected by the township's Tax Collector, who also runs the township sewer accounts. The office is in Room 108 of the municipal building at 820 Mercer Street, and the phone is 856-488-7880. It also acts as the collecting agent for the public school district, the fire district and Camden County, so one bill covers all of them.

Value is a separate matter. The township assessor sets assessments, appeals go to the Camden County Board of Taxation in Blackwood, and the collector has no role in them. The township's main number is 856-665-6500, and the assessor and collector both work from 820 Mercer Street. The collector tells you what you owe. The assessor and county board tell you whether the value behind it can be challenged.

Cherry Hill at a glance

The township spreads over 24.07 square miles in northern Camden County and had an estimated 79,965 residents in 2025. Home values center on $386,300, and 76.5 percent of homes are owner-occupied. Neighborhood names buyers search by include Erlton, Barclay, Kingston, Greentree, Springdale, Old Orchard, Woodcrest and Ellisburg.

Interstate 295 has three exits in the township, and Routes 38, 41, 70 and 154 cross it. The PATCO station at Woodcrest and NJ Transit's Atlantic City Line stop give commuters a route into Philadelphia. The school district runs 19 schools, which is a draw for families and shows up in how listings are marketed.

Due dates, interest and where the money goes

The township's quarterly dates are August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. A ten-day cushion follows each one, and a tenth day that falls on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday carries the cushion to the next working day. The office mails bills twice a year: in July for the third and fourth quarters and in January for the first and second. A bill that never shows up does not cancel the payment or the interest.

Money has to reach the office before the grace period ends, because New Jersey does not allow the collector to accept postmarks. Once the cushion ends, interest is charged retroactively: 8 percent annually on the first slice of $1,500 behind, 18 percent annually on the remainder. Balances still open can move into the tax sale process, which has to be finished by June 30, and payments during that period must be cash or a cashier's check.

How to pay a tax or sewer bill

  • Drop off cash or a check at Room 108, or use the mail slot on the double doors at the entrance if the building is closed.
  • Mail a check to the Tax Collector's Office, 820 Mercer Street, Cherry Hill, NJ 08002.

  • Use your bank's bill-pay with "Township of Cherry Hill" as payee and your numeric account number only.
  • Pay by phone: 855-472-2993 for taxes and 855-472-2990 for sewer.

The counter and the staff phone line do not take cards. The office also sends email reminders about a week before each due date to residents who sign up.

Sewer charges and the senior discount

A flat annual fee covers residential sewer and falls due April 1. Commercial sewer follows water use and is billed in two parts, due the first of November and the first of May. A 10 percent reduction is available to owners aged 60 and up who live in the house and show the Tax Collector proof of age. Sewer is billed apart from tax, so the closing agent should ask the collector whether it is paid to date.

Is a Cherry Hill assessment open to challenge?

Yes. Camden County's tax board hears the case, with filing closing April 1 or, right after a township revaluation, May 1. The petition has to reach the county before close of business that day, and installments through the first quarter stay payable while the case is open. Evidence is up to five comparable sales, since neighbors' assessments carry no weight. With the average assessment at $227,000, you have a yardstick when you compare your notice to the street around you.

Appeal only the value, never the amount of tax. Your argument is what the house was worth on the October 1 that precedes the tax year, set against the town's average ratio. If the county board lowers the value, that judgment holds for the year and the two that follow unless a revaluation or an added assessment changes it. After the board rules, the Tax Court of New Jersey takes any further case, filed within 45 days.

Selling with tax still owed

A sale can go ahead with tax owing, because the balance is cleared out of the seller's money at the table. Request a payoff statement dated for your closing day, and hand the latest bill to the title company so the next installment goes to the right place.

  • Look at where your closing date sits against the next quarter and its cushion.
  • Confirm the sewer account is paid to date.
  • If a lien has been sold at the tax sale, the lien holder is the party owed the redemption amount.

A cash sale does not change any of this. It only removes the lender's appraisal and most repairs, so the payoff letters and the sewer check become the main items on your list.

Getting ready to sell a Cherry Hill house

Order the tax payoff and the sewer status together, since both come from the same office. Compare your assessment notice with the house, and check the date of the next quarter against your closing date. If the closing falls near a due date, ask the closing agent whether to pay the installment first or have it handled from your proceeds.

Keep the latest bill, because the title company needs it to place the next installment. If you are 60 or older and live in the house, carry proof of age to the collector so the sewer discount is not lost in the transition.

Ten days from each due date, stretched past a weekend or holiday to the next working day. The office has to have the money in hand by then, as postmarks carry no weight.

Where do I pay Cherry Hill taxes?

Pay at the Tax Collector's Office, 820 Mercer Street, Room 108, by mail, online, by phone or through bank bill-pay. Call 856-488-7880 for help.

Does Cherry Hill offer a sewer discount for seniors?

Yes. A 10 percent cut on the residential sewer fee goes to owner-occupants aged 60 or more who show proof of age.

How much interest does Cherry Hill charge on late tax?

Eight percent per year covers the first $1,500 late and 18 percent the rest, charged back to the original due date.

Who hears a Cherry Hill assessment appeal?

The county board in Blackwood, at 509 Lakeland Road. Filing closes April 1, or May 1 when the township has just completed a revaluation.

Who bills you and who sets your value

Two offices at 33 Washington Street split the work. The Tax Collector sends the bill and takes payment, and the Tax Assessor sets the value the bill is built on. The counter is open weekdays from 8:30 am to 4:30 pm. A dispute over value does not stay in the building: it goes to the Ocean County Board of Taxation, which supervises the assessor.

Toms River has been a calendar year town since January 2010, so the tax year matches the calendar and bills go out in July. If you are listing a house, expect the closing figures to rest on the current calendar year, divided into four installments.

Toms River housing and prices

Toms River is a shore township and the seat of Ocean County. The 2020 census counted 95,438 people, and a 2025 federal estimate puts the figure at 100,899. How to contest your assessment

Appeals go to the Ocean County Board of Taxation, and the filing window closes April 1. A township-wide revaluation or reassessment moves that cutoff to May 1. For filing questions the assessor sends you to the board at 732-929-2008.

The assessor's FAQ makes two points. An appeal challenges your assessed value and has no effect on the tax bill itself, because the township, school district, county and fire districts set the budgets, not the assessor or the county board. And comparable assessments do not count as evidence of market value; only comparable sales do. Gather closed sale prices for similar Toms River houses before you file.

If you built or added something and received an Added Assessment bill, the appeal deadline is December 1 of the year the added assessment was placed. The date of the Certificate of Occupancy does not set the assessment date, because a home is valued when it is substantially ready for its intended use.

Deductions and relief programs

Qualified recipients receive a $250 deduction from the annual tax bill. Eligible groups are disabled persons, senior citizens, surviving spouses, veteran homeowners and the widows of veteran owners. Applications go through the Tax Assessor at 732-341-1000, extension 8300.

Two state programs also exist, the Property Tax Reimbursement Program and the Homestead Rebate Program. Ask the state Division of Taxation about eligibility and payment status. If you claim a deduction now, mention it to your attorney so the closing figures reflect it.

Selling with taxes owed

When taxes go unpaid, the township can sell a tax lien, which the owner or a mortgage holder can later redeem. Only a party with legal interest, meaning the owner, the owner's attorney or the mortgage holder, may redeem, and the request must be in writing. Verbal requests are refused.

The redemption statement takes time to prepare, so ask early in the sale. No new bill is issued when ownership changes, so hand the existing bill to the new owner at closing. A buyer left without one can ask the Tax Collector for a copy or print it from the township's online account lookup.

If a lender escrows your taxes and the loan ends at closing, the township wants written notice so the bank comes off its records. The notice needs the block and lot number, your mailing address, the bank's name and address, and the owner's signature. Skipping this step can leave a buyer with a duplicate bill and confusion over who paid the next quarter.

A seller's checklist for Toms River

Start with the Tax Collector: ask which installments are paid, whether any lien exists, and what the payoff looks like through your closing date. Next, confirm whether any deduction is on the account, since the Tax Assessor handles those applications. If a bank escrows your taxes, send the written notice with block and lot, your address and the bank's details, signed by the owner.

On closing day, give the buyer the current bill. Because Toms River collects by quarter, the closing agent normally divides the open installment between you and the buyer. A cash buyer purchasing as is skips the appraisal and loan approval wait, but the same tax steps apply, so none of this paperwork can be skipped.

Frequently asked questions

Which phone number reaches the Toms River tax office?

Dial 732-341-1000 and ask for extension 8342 to reach the collector. Lines are staffed on weekdays and get busy near due dates, so leave a message. Value questions use extension 8300.

Does Toms River allow extra days after a due date?

Yes, ten days. A Saturday, Sunday or holiday on day ten pushes the deadline one business day later. Bank bill-pay checks can take several days to arrive, so send them early.

By what date must a Toms River owner file an assessment appeal?

April 1, moving to May 1 in a year with a township revaluation or reassessment. The county board takes the filing. Appeals of an Added Assessment close December 1.

Can I sell a Toms River house that has a tax lien on it?

Yes. The payoff comes out of proceeds, and a written redemption statement from the Tax Collector sets the figure. Only the owner, the owner's attorney or the mortgage holder may ask for it, and it takes time to prepare.

Does the new owner get a new tax bill after the sale?

No. The township mails no replacement when ownership changes, so the seller hands the existing bill to the buyer. The buyer can print a duplicate through the township's online tax account inquiry.

Two cutoffs apply. A petition on an added or omitted assessment has to reach the board in person by 4:15 p.m. on December 1, shifting to the next business day if that is a weekend or holiday. An owner denied a senior or disabled deduction files Form A-1 by the following April 1.

An owner who is 65 or older, or disabled, may take $250 off the annual bill after a year of New Jersey residence. The rules also look at ownership and occupancy on October 1 of the pretax year, an on-time application and an income limit.

The first two quarters are set at half of last year's bill, while the last two reflect the rate struck for the current year. If the budgets of the county, school district and township rose, the second half grows, and if they fell it shrinks.

Ten days after the first of February, May, August or November. After that, taxes are delinquent and interest is counted from the first day of the quarter.

The winter bill is a preliminary figure near half of last year's taxes. The summer bill applies the new rate for the year and subtracts the preliminary amount already billed.

Old Bridge covers 38.18 square miles of land in the Raritan Valley, faces Staten Island across Raritan Bay and sits roughly 25 miles from New York City. Deed filing happens at the Middlesex County Clerk, whose office can give the current fee schedule. The collector can issue a payoff letter good through the closing date. All of Old Bridge Township lies within the Old Bridge school district, so school boundaries are the same across the township.

When you sell, the contract usually divides the quarter in which you close between you and the buyer by the day. Your attorney will explain how it is done, and the settlement statement shows your share.

Because the grace period is only 10 days and e-checks can take 10 business days to clear, sellers who pay close to the deadline should use a method that posts quickly. A late installment adds interest to the payoff, and that number is what the title company will collect from your proceeds.

Middletown's installments land on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. A 10-day grace period normally follows, and if day ten is a weekend or holiday the cutoff slides to the next business day. Pay by 3:45 PM on the last grace day to avoid interest.

The aggregate preliminary net value of Middletown for tax year 2026 was 7.94% above 2025. Monmouth County uses an alternate calendar, so the appeal deadline is January 15, or April 1 if the assessment exceeds $1 million. The statewide April 1 date does not govern ordinary houses here. Petitions can be filed through secure.njappealonline.com.

Before filing, compare your value with closed sales on the township's interactive sales map, which leaves out distressed sales. Only the assessment can be appealed, not the tax, and evidence should be dated before the October 1 assessment date.

Historic districts and a sale

The township's Landmarks Commission reviews work on structures inside the five historic districts: Chapel Hill, Locust, Monmouth Hills, Navesink and Middletown Village. Owners planning additions or changes need a Certificate of Appropriateness. A buyer of a house in one of those districts should know that exterior plans may go through that review.

  • Find out if the parcel has entered the tax sale process, because extra costs and guaranteed funds are then required.
  • Check any sewer balance with the Sewerage Authority, which keeps its own account.
  • Get the written figures to the title company and your attorney well before closing.

A cash buyer can shorten the timeline, but the payoff, any lien and the recording steps remain. Because bills go out once a year and the second-half amount is not known until the rate is set, ask the collector what has been billed so far and what is still to come, so the title company can split the year fairly between you and the buyer.

January 15, or April 1 when the assessment is over $1 million. Monmouth County follows an alternate calendar, and filing can be done through secure.njappealonline.com.

Call the Township of Middletown Sewerage Authority at 732-495-1010. Delinquent sewer charges are separate from the property tax bill.
